--- title: "Week 08: Multiple Regression I" subtitle: "Date: October 15, 2026" footer: "[course-website](https://dharaden.github.io/psyc640/)" logo: "images/640_hex.png" format: revealjs: theme: [default, brand, clean.scss] multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: true incremental: false chalkboard: true overview: false scrollable: true code-line-numbers: true editor: visual execute: echo: true freeze: auto editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- ## Today... **One predictor was never the plan.** - Why a second predictor changes the first one's meaning - "Holding constant" — what it actually does - A slope that **flips sign** when we add the right variable - Did the new predictor earn its place? ($\Delta R^2$, nested $F$) - *b* or *β*: which one do you report? - When predictors step on each other (multicollinearity) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(here) library(tidyverse) library(rio) library(broom) library(psych) options(scipen = 999) ``` ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Where we have been | Week | Model | What was new | |------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------| | 5 | $Y = b_0 + b_1X$ | one continuous predictor | | 6 | $Y = b_0 + b_1D$ | the predictor can be a **group** | | 7 | $SS_{total} = SS_{model} + SS_{res}$ | how well the line fits | . . . Everything so far has been **one predictor at a time**. That is almost never the model you want. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The only equation we need $$Y_i = b_0 + b_1X_{1i} + b_2X_{2i} + \dots + b_kX_{ki} + e_i$$ ::: incremental - $b_0$ — predicted $Y$ when **every** predictor is 0 - $b_1$ — change in $Y$ per 1-unit change in $X_1$, **holding the other predictors constant** - $e_i$ — still the part we miss ::: . . . ::: callout-important That phrase — *holding the other predictors constant* — is the entire week. It is not decoration. It changes what the number means. ::: # Part 1: Why Bother? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## You have been hired by the county 🚒 The fire department wants to know what drives the **cost of a fire**. They hand you 300 fires: how many **trucks** were dispatched, how many **acres** burned, and the **damage** in thousands of dollars. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(640) n <- 300 acres <- round(runif(n, 0.5, 40), 1) trucks <- round(1 + 0.22 * acres + rnorm(n, 0, 1.2)) trucks[trucks < 1] <- 1 damage <- 10 + 4.2 * acres - 2.8 * trucks + rnorm(n, 0, 12) fire <- tibble(acres, trucks, damage) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} glimpse(fire) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 300 Columns: 3 $ acres 10.3, 8.0, 29.4, 31.7, 8.0, 25.9, 12.5, 38.6, 29.3, 14.0, 32.1,… $ trucks 1, 3, 8, 7, 2, 7, 2, 10, 8, 3, 6, 6, 8, 8, 1, 4, 1, 6, 7, 11, 1… $ damage 68.4656354, 29.8639841, 98.0352116, 123.1168377, 42.6368658, 10… ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Start where we always start ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} fire %>% ggplot(aes(x = trucks, y = damage)) + geom_point(alpha = .5) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#B3261E") + labs(x = "Trucks dispatched", y = "Damage ($1,000s)") + theme_bw(base_size = 16) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-08_multiple-reg_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fire_one <- lm(damage ~ trucks, data = fire) tidy(fire_one) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 8.84 3.28 2.70 7.41e- 3 2 trucks 12.7 0.515 24.7 3.53e-74 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## What would you tell the county? ::: incremental - *b* = **12.73**: each additional truck is associated with **\$12,730 more** damage - $p$ \< .001, $R^2$ = .67 — this is not a fragile finding ::: . . . > "Trucks strongly predict damage. **Send fewer trucks.**" . . . ::: callout-warning Every number in that sentence is correct. The recommendation would get people killed. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 🧠 Side quest: draw the thing {background-color="#EFE6F7"} Before you fit anything, sketch what you think is going on. Arrows for "causes." - Does `trucks` → `damage`? - Does something cause **both**? . . . A variable that causes both your predictor and your outcome is a **confound**. Leave it out and your slope absorbs its effect. These sketches have a name. Remember when we talked about **Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG's)**? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The variable we ignored ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} fire %>% ggplot(aes(x = trucks, y = damage, color = acres)) + geom_point(alpha = .8) + scale_color_viridis_c(option = "inferno", direction = -1) + labs(x = "Trucks dispatched", y = "Damage ($1,000s)", color = "Acres\nburned") + theme_bw(base_size = 16) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-08_multiple-reg_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Big fires get more trucks **and** do more damage. The slope we estimated was mostly **fire size wearing a truck costume**. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Put acres in the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fire_two <- lm(damage ~ trucks + acres, data = fire) tidy(fire_two) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 10.9 1.65 6.62 1.64e-10 2 trucks -2.63 0.579 -4.54 8.16e- 6 3 acres 4.09 0.138 29.6 9.72e-91 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: incremental - `trucks`: **+12.73 → −2.63**. The sign *flipped*. - `acres`: +4.09 per acre - $R^2$: .672 → **.917** ::: . . . Each additional truck is associated with **\$2,630 less** damage — **among fires of the same size**. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## What just happened ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Before** We compared a 2-truck fire to a 9-truck fire. Those are not the same fire. One was a kitchen; one was a neighborhood. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **After** We compare 2-truck and 3-truck fires **of the same acreage**. Now the extra truck can only help. ::: ::::: . . . ::: callout-important ## "Holding constant" is a comparison, not a magic word $b_1$ answers: among cases that are **identical on every other predictor in the model**, what is the difference in $Y$ per unit of $X_1$? Identical on the predictors you *included*. Nothing else. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Omitted variables do not politely disappear When you leave out a variable that is related to both $X$ and $Y$, its effect does not vanish — it gets **folded into** the coefficients you did estimate. ::: incremental - Sometimes the slope is **inflated** (the trucks case) - Sometimes it is **shrunk** (next week's tutoring example) - Sometimes it appears out of nowhere (Lab 8's suppression) - Sometimes **nothing moves** — and that is a finding too ::: . . . You cannot tell which from the output. You can only tell from **what you chose to measure**. # Part 2: Real Data, Real Stakes ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 520 students, one survey 😵‍💫 A student-stress survey: everything rated 1–5. The column names are, charitably, a disaster — so we rename by position. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stress <- import(here("files", "data", "student_stress.xlsx")) %>% set_names(c("sleep_quality", "headaches", "academic_perf", "study_load", "extracurricular", "stress")) stress %>% describe(fast = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` vars n mean sd median min max range skew kurtosis se sleep_quality 1 520 3.12 1.10 3.0 1 5 4 0.01 -0.66 0.05 headaches 2 520 2.18 1.25 2.0 1 5 4 0.75 -0.48 0.05 academic_perf 3 520 3.33 1.06 3.0 1 5 4 -0.34 -0.28 0.05 study_load 4 520 2.75 1.37 2.5 1 5 4 0.23 -1.25 0.06 extracurricular 5 520 2.68 1.47 3.0 1 5 4 0.32 -1.26 0.06 stress 6 520 2.88 1.36 3.0 1 5 4 0.09 -1.18 0.06 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Who correlates with stress? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stress %>% cor() %>% round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sleep_quality headaches academic_perf study_load sleep_quality 1.000 -0.059 0.254 0.065 headaches -0.059 1.000 -0.205 -0.007 academic_perf 0.254 -0.205 1.000 0.096 study_load 0.065 -0.007 0.096 1.000 extracurricular 0.001 -0.073 0.153 0.175 stress 0.165 -0.072 0.055 0.392 extracurricular stress sleep_quality 0.001 0.165 headaches -0.073 -0.072 academic_perf 0.153 0.055 study_load 0.175 0.392 extracurricular 1.000 0.052 stress 0.052 1.000 ``` ::: ::: . . . ## Well that doesn't look nice... ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Who correlates with stress? (but looks nice) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stress %>% sjPlot::tab_corr(var.labels = c("Sleep Quality", "Headaches", "Academic Performance", "Study Load", "Extracurricular", "Stress"), triangle = "lower") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
  Sleep Quality Headaches Academic Performance Study Load Extracurricular Stress
Sleep Quality            
Headaches -0.059          
Academic Performance 0.254*** -0.205***        
Study Load 0.065 -0.007 0.096*      
Extracurricular 0.001 -0.073 0.153*** 0.175***    
Stress 0.165*** -0.072 0.055 0.392*** 0.052  
Computed correlation used pearson-method with listwise-deletion.
````` ::: ::: ::: incremental - `study_load` is the obvious candidate: *r* = **.39** - `sleep_quality` is next: *r* = **.17** - And the two predictors barely know each other: *r* = **.065** ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Model 1: study load alone ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} s_one <- lm(stress ~ study_load, data = stress) tidy(s_one) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 1.81 0.123 14.7 3.11e-41 2 study_load 0.387 0.0400 9.69 1.66e-20 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} glance(s_one) %>% select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 r.squared adj.r.squared sigma 1 0.153 0.152 1.25 ``` ::: ::: . . . Each 1-point increase in study load → **0.39** points more stress. $R^2$ = **.153**. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Model 2: add sleep quality ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} s_two <- lm(stress ~ study_load + sleep_quality, data = stress) tidy(s_two) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 1.29 0.191 6.76 3.78e-11 2 study_load 0.378 0.0397 9.54 5.55e-20 3 sleep_quality 0.173 0.0495 3.50 5.00e- 4 ``` ::: ::: . . . | Predictor | Alone | Together | |-----------------|-------|-----------| | `study_load` | 0.388 | **0.378** | | `sleep_quality` | — | **0.174** | The study-load slope moved by **0.01**. Essentially nothing. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Why nothing moved A coefficient only changes when the new predictor is related to **both** the outcome and the old predictor. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cor.test(stress$study_load, stress$sleep_quality) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson's product-moment correlation data: stress$study_load and stress$sleep_quality t = 1.4933, df = 518, p-value = 0.136 alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: -0.0206320 0.1506088 sample estimates: cor 0.0654704 ``` ::: ::: ::: incremental - *r* = .065 → the two predictors carry **separate** information - So each one keeps the effect it had on its own - Their contributions simply **add** ::: . . . ::: callout-tip "I added a predictor and the first one didn't budge" is a **real result**, and it is the common one. It means your two predictors are not competing for the same variance. Say that, instead of apologizing for it. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Interpreting Model 2 out loud $$\widehat{Stress} = 1.29 + 0.378(StudyLoad) + 0.174(SleepQuality)$$ ::: incremental - **1.29** — predicted stress for a student who rated study load *and* sleep quality as 0. **Neither is possible** (the scale starts at 1), so this intercept is a mathematical anchor, not a person. - **0.378** — comparing two students with the **same sleep quality**, one point more study load goes with 0.38 points more stress - **0.174** — comparing two students with the **same study load**, one point more sleep quality goes with 0.17 points more stress ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Wait. Read that last one again. 🤨 **Better sleep quality predicts *more* stress** (*b* = +0.174, *p* \< .001), holding study load constant. . . . Three possibilities, and you cannot choose between them from this output: ::: incremental 1. The item is scored **backwards** — maybe 5 means "I rate my sleep quality as a problem" 2. The relationship is real and reflects something else (students who sleep well take on more) 3. The survey question was ambiguous and students interpreted it inconsistently ::: . . . ::: callout-important This is the midterm's lesson arriving in a lecture. **Check the direction of every coefficient against what you expected.** When it disagrees, the first suspect is always scoring — not the universe. ::: # Part 3: Did It Earn Its Place? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Three ways to ask the same question ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} glance(s_one) %>% select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 r.squared adj.r.squared sigma 1 0.153 0.152 1.25 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} glance(s_two) %>% select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 r.squared adj.r.squared sigma 1 0.173 0.170 1.24 ``` ::: ::: | Model | $R^2$ | adj. $R^2$ | RSE | |------------------|-----------|------------|------------| | study load | .1534 | .1517 | 1.2506 | | \+ sleep quality | **.1730** | **.1698** | **1.2372** | ::: incremental - $\Delta R^2$ = **.0196** — about 2% more of stress accounted for - Adjusted $R^2$ went **up**, so the predictor paid its own df - Typical miss shrank from 1.251 to 1.237 (on a variable with SD = 1.358) ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The formal test: nested models Model 1 is **nested** inside Model 2 — same data, same outcome, Model 1 is Model 2 with one coefficient forced to zero. That lets us test the difference directly. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(s_one, s_two) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: stress ~ study_load Model 2: stress ~ study_load + sleep_quality Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 518 810.12 2 517 791.34 1 18.779 12.269 0.0005005 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Reading that table | Column | What it is | Here | |-------------|---------------------------------|-----------------| | `Res.Df` | df left after estimating | 518 → 517 | | `RSS` | unexplained SS | 810.12 → 791.34 | | `Df` | predictors added | 1 | | `Sum of Sq` | SS the new predictor picked up | **18.78** | | `F` | is that drop bigger than noise? | **12.27** | | `Pr(>F)` | the *p*-value | **.0005** | . . . With one added predictor, this $F$ is just the square of its $t$: $3.503^2 = 12.27$. Same test, different table. ✅ ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Now let's add three useless things ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} s_junk <- lm(stress ~ study_load + sleep_quality + extracurricular + headaches + academic_perf, data = stress) tidy(s_junk) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 1.59 0.275 5.80 1.13e- 8 2 study_load 0.383 0.0404 9.50 8.00e-20 3 sleep_quality 0.178 0.0512 3.47 5.68e- 4 4 extracurricular -0.0148 0.0380 -0.389 6.97e- 1 5 headaches -0.0740 0.0445 -1.66 9.73e- 2 6 academic_perf -0.0384 0.0547 -0.703 4.83e- 1 ``` ::: ::: Extracurriculars (*p* = .70), headaches (*p* = .10), academic performance (*p* = .48). ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Watch the two R²s diverge | Model | $R^2$ | adj. $R^2$ | RSE | |--------------|--------------|--------------|--------| | 2 predictors | .1730 | .1698 | 1.2372 | | 5 predictors | **.1779** ⬆️ | **.1699** ➡️ | 1.2371 | ::: incremental - $R^2$ rose by .005, because **it always rises** - Adjusted $R^2$ moved by **.0001** — three predictors bought you nothing - RSE: unchanged to four decimals ::: . . . ::: callout-important Week 7's warning, now with consequences. $R^2$ cannot tell you whether a predictor belongs in the model. **Adjusted** $R^2$, the nested $F$, and your theory can. ::: # Part 4: Reporting It ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## *b* or *β*? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stress %>% mutate(across(everything(), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)))) %>% lm(stress ~ study_load + sleep_quality, data = .) %>% tidy() %>% select(term, estimate) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 term estimate 1 (Intercept) 1.26e-16 2 study_load 3.82e- 1 3 sleep_quality 1.40e- 1 ``` ::: ::: ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Report *b* when** - the units mean something (dollars, hours, mg) - you want to compare predictors **within** this sample ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Report *β* when** - the units are arbitrary (survey points) - you want to compare **across** studies or scales ::: ::::: . . . Here: β = **.38** vs **.14**. Study load matters roughly **2.7×** as much as sleep quality for stress. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## When predictors step on each other If two predictors are nearly the same variable, the model cannot tell them apart. Coefficients get unstable and standard errors balloon. **VIF** (variance inflation factor) measures it: $VIF_j = \frac{1}{1 - R^2_j}$, where $R^2_j$ is from regressing predictor $j$ on all the others. With two predictors you can compute it by hand — regress one predictor on the other: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # stress model 1 / (1 - summary(lm(study_load ~ sleep_quality, data = stress))$r.squared) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.004305 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # fire model 1 / (1 - summary(lm(trucks ~ acres, data = fire))$r.squared) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.997326 ``` ::: ::: ::: incremental - Stress model: VIF = **1.004** — these predictors are strangers - Fire model: VIF = **5.00** — acres and trucks are nearly redundant (*r* = .89), and the SE on `trucks` rose from 0.515 to 0.579 as a result ::: . . . Rules of thumb: \> 5 is worth a sentence, \> 10 is a problem. Note that the fire model still **worked** — high VIF widens your SEs, it does not invalidate the model. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Checking the Model - Easy There are a lot of ways to take a look at the model One of the easiest ways is to use `performance` and their `check_model()` function ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} performance::check_model(s_junk) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-08_multiple-reg_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The write-up > [Stress was regressed on self-reported study load and sleep quality]{.underline} in a sample of 520 students. The overall model was significant, *F*(2, 517) = 54.07, *p* \< .001, accounting for 17.3% of the variance in stress (adj. *R²* = .170). Holding sleep quality constant, each one-point increase in study load was associated with a 0.38-point increase in stress (*b* = 0.38, *SE* = 0.04, *t* = 9.54, *p* \< .001). Holding study load constant, each one-point increase in rated sleep quality was associated with a 0.17-point increase in stress (*b* = 0.17, *SE* = 0.05, *t* = 3.50, *p* \< .001). Adding sleep quality improved fit over study load alone, Δ*R²* = .020, *F*(1, 517) = 12.27, *p* \< .001. The positive coefficient for sleep quality was contrary to expectation and may reflect the direction in which that item was scored. . . . ::: callout-tip Everything a reader needs: the overall test, each coefficient **with its holding-constant clause**, the model comparison, and an honest flag on the odd result. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 🛠️ Activity: Does Spending More Make More? ::: callout-tip **Week 8 Exercises** · \~45 min · Pairs ::: 1,763 films, 1970–2013: budget, international gross, year, and whether the film passes the Bechdel test. - Budget alone explains **35%** of gross - Add **one** more variable and the budget slope gets *bigger* - You will find out why, and write it up like a consultant [Open the activity](../class-activities/wk8_multiple-reg.html){.button target="_blank"} ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## ✍️ Wrap-Up Finish these at the bottom of your activity file: 1. In your own words: what does "holding X constant" let you compare? 2. A colleague says "my $R^2$ went up, so the new predictor helped." What do you ask them for? 3. One thing that is still muddy → journal. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## For next time ::: callout-important ## 📂 Midterm Project — due Tuesday 10/27 at 11:59pm **Part 6 is now unlocked.** You have everything you need: the two-predictor model, the "holding constant" interpretation, $\Delta R^2$, and the model-comparison table. Target for this weekend: Parts 1–5 done, Part 6 drafted. That leaves next week for writing instead of panicking. ::: **No lab is due this week or next** — the midterm is the assignment. 📖 Chapter 14.3 — ST · Chapter 8.1 — MSR **Next week:** what happens when the groups from Week 6 meet the predictors from this week — and what to do when a slope is *different* for different groups.
